title: SpeeDiff: Scalable Pixel-Anchored End-to-End Latent Diffusion Model

paper.title: SpeeDiff: Scalable Pixel-Anchored End-to-End Latent Diffusion Model
paper.abstract:
Abstract We present S calable P ixel-anchored E nd-to- e nd Diff usion (SpeeDiff), a latent diffusion method that jointly trains the VAE and the diffusion model from scratch. In principle, joint training allows the diffusion loss gradient to directly guide the VAE encoder, encouraging the formation of a generation-friendly latent space and potentially yielding faster convergence than the conventional two-stage approach with a pretrained frozen VAE. However, a naive end-to-end implementation severely degrades performance, as unrestricted backpropagation of the diffusion loss leads to latent space collapse.
Our main technical contribution is a simple yet effective Tweedie Pixel Reconstruction (TPR) loss, which provides additional pixel-level feedback by decoding a predicted clean latent from an intermediate noisy state using Tweedie’s formula, thereby alleviating collapse. Furthermore, our method enables jointly scaling a fully transformer-based architecture and enhances representation alignment within the end-to-end framework.
Our SpeeDiff-XL model achieves over 140 × \times and 61 × \times faster training compared to Vanilla SiT and REPA, respectively, while attaining an FID of 1.50 without guidance on ImageNet 256 × \times 256 generation. With a more efficient 32 × \times compressed VAE, our model further reaches an FID of 1.53 without guidance on ImageNet 512 × \times 512 generation.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Latent diffusion models (LDMs) [ 54 , 46 , 41 ] have emerged as a dominant paradigm for visual synthesis. These models perform the diffusion process in a compact latent space produced by a visual tokenizer, typically a variational autoencoder (VAE) [ 28 ] . In the standard two-stage training pipeline, the visual tokenizer is first trained to encode raw visual data into a compressed latent space, after which a diffusion model is learned to operate within that latent domain while keeping the pretrained visual tokenizer frozen. Recent advances in LDMs have largely focused on enhancing the VAEs by leveraging vision foundation models (VFMs) [ 40 , 50 , 45 , 61 , 18 ] . Despite their success, VAEs trained with reconstruction objectives primarily capture low-level pixel statistics, resulting in latent spaces that do not directly associate with sufficient semantic knowledge, posing challenges for the diffusion model to learn efficiently. Motivated by semantically rich representations from self-supervise pretrained VFMs, recent works either incorporate representation alignment to a VFM [ 58 , 33 ] or directly replace the VAE encoder with a VFM [ 63 , 49 , 3 , 5 ] . These approaches have achieved remarkable improvements in training efficiency and generative quality. In contrast to improving the visual tokenizer through VFMs, much less attention has been given to enhancing it via end-to-end optimization with direct feedback from the diffusion model training. This idea can in fact be traced back to LSGM [ 54 ] , where the VAE and diffusion model were jointly trained. However, vanilla end-to-end training was found to degrade overall performance, a phenomenon that has also been revisited in recent studies [ 33 ] . We believe that enabling truly end-to-end optimization holds the potential to further push the performance limits of LDMs, yet existing approaches still lack effective mechanisms to support that. In this paper, we focus on the core idea of enhancing the VAE through end-to-end direct gradient feedback from diffusion training , and show that allowing the latent space to evolve under generative supervision further improves both training efficiency and synthesis quality. After carefully analyzing the vanilla end-to-end training, we find that the diffusion loss tends to collapse the latent space into a degenerate representation. Specifically, we observe that the latent statistics exhibit severely suppressed per-channel variances and large per-channel biass (see Fig. 3 ). We further demonstrate that this latent collapse can be effectively alleviated with a simple Tweedie Pixel Reconstruction (TPR) loss, which computes a pixel-level reconstruction loss by decoding the predicted clean latent from an intermediate noisy state using Tweedie’s formula [ 9 ] . Extensive experiments show that this additional pixel-level feedback anchors the VAE and prevents latent degeneracy, resulting in robust and well-converged end-to-end training. Building upon the end-to-end training framework, we further improve latent diffusion model through two enhancements. We first refine the architecture by replacing the conventional convolutional VAE (CNN-VAE) with a vision-transformer-based variant (ViT-VAE) and modernizing the diffusion backbone (DiT [ 41 , 37 ] ) with recent architectural improvements. In addition, inspired by REPA [ 60 , 33 ] , we introduce REPA++ , a enhanced representation alignment method in our end-to-end training that aligns both the latent and the intermediate diffusion features with VFM representations (e.g., DINOv3 [ 50 ] ) and is optimized end-to-end with both diffusion and VAE. Our final method, SpeeDiff, is a single-stage end-to-end latent diffusion framework that jointly trains the VAE and diffusion model from scratch without stop-gradient operations (see Fig. 1 b), simplifying the conventional two-stage pipeline while substantially accelerating diffusion convergence (see Fig. 1 c) and improving scaling effect (see Fig. 1 d). To assess the contribution of representation alignment, we compare SpeeDiff variants with and without REPA++. The model without alignment achieves an FID of 2.42, setting a new state-of-the-art among methods that do not rely on VFM alignment, whereas incorporating REPA++ further reduces the FID to 1.50. For ImageNet 512 × \times 512, SpeeDiff-XL model using a efficient 32 × \times compressed VAE achieves an FID of 1.53 without guidance. Figure 2 : Detailed training pipeline of SpeeDiff. The forward pass consists of four major branches: (1) Reconstruction branch: ℒ VAE \mathcal{L}_{\text{VAE}} is computed over reconstructions from the VAE encoder and decoder. (2) Diffusion branch: follows the standard stochastic interpolant and leverages flow prediction as diffusion loss. (3) Tweedie Pixel Reconstruction branch: clean latents are estimated via Tweedie’s formula, decoded, and compared against ground-truth images. (4) REPA++ branch: both latents and intermediate diffusion features are aligned with VFM representations. Notably, SpeeDiff doesn’t requires stop-gradient operation and train both VAE and diffusion from scratch.

sections.heading: Variational autoencoder as tokenizer.
sections.text: Visual tokenizers employ either continuous [ 46 , 32 ] , discrete [ 10 , 36 ] , or unified [ 55 , 35 ] latent representations. We focus on continuous tokenizers for visual generation, which are predominantly implemented using variational autoencoders (VAEs) [ 28 , 46 ] . Such VAE-based tokenizers have become a fundamental component of modern text-to-image and video generation systems [ 32 , 15 , 43 , 29 , 55 ] . To achieve better fidelity, the reconstruction term is often complemented with perceptual loss [ 62 , 12 ] and adversarial loss [ 16 , 10 ] .

sections.heading: Representation from VFMs.
sections.text: Recent studies show that incorporating semantic representations from self-supervise pretrained vision foundation models (VFMs), such as DINO [ 40 , 50 ] , CLIP [ 45 ] and MAE [ 18 ] , can substantially improve the convergence and generative quality of diffusion models. Depending on how VFMs are utilized, existing approaches fall into two main categories: representation alignment and direct representation utilization. The representation alignment family [ 60 , 33 , 58 ] distills VFM semantics by enforcing consistency between latent (or intermediate diffusion features) and VFM representations. For instance, REPA [ 60 ] employs a cosine-similarity objective, whereas VA-VAE [ 58 ] adopts a more sophisticated similarity loss. REPA-E [ 33 ] backpropagates a representation alignment loss through from diffusion to VAE encoder. In contrast, another line of work [ 63 , 49 , 3 , 5 ] replaces the VAE encoder with a pretrained VFM and directly leverages its representation as the latent, with different design choices such as freezing the tokenizer in RAE [ 63 ] , adding a learnable residual module in SVG [ 49 ] , or inserting a learnable projection layer in VFM-VAE [ 3 ] . To better integrate VFMs into our end-to-end training paradigm as a flexible plug-and-play module, we adopt the representation alignment strategy and introduce REPA++ , an enhanced alignment mechanism in our end-to-end training framework. sections.heading: 3 Our Approach
sections.text: We now outline the key components of our approach. We first analyze the vanilla end-to-end training ( Sec. 3.1 ) and identify latent collapse as the primary cause of failure. To address this issue, we introduce a simple yet effective Tweedie Pixel Reconstruction loss that provides additional pixel-level feedback ( Sec. 3.2 ). We then enhance the framework with refined architectures and REPA++ ( Sec. 3.3 , Sec. 3.4 ) to accelerate convergence and improve final performance.

sections.heading: 3.1 Vanilla End-to-end Training
sections.text: The vanilla end-to-end setup directly couples the VAE and diffusion model by optimizing both objectives simultaneously from scratch: ℒ Vanilla-E2E ​ ( ϕ , 𝝍 , 𝜽 ) = ℒ VAE ​ ( ϕ , 𝝍 ) + ℒ Diff ​ ( ϕ , 𝜽 ) , \mathcal{L}_{\text{Vanilla-E2E}}({\bm{\phi}},{\bm{\psi}},{\bm{\theta}})=\mathcal{L}_{\text{VAE}}({\bm{\phi}},{\bm{\psi}})+\mathcal{L}_{\text{Diff}}({\bm{\phi}},{\bm{\theta}}), (1) where ϕ {\bm{\phi}} , 𝝍 {\bm{\psi}} and 𝜽 {\bm{\theta}} refers to the parameters of VAE encoder, VAE decoder and diffusion, respectively. Despite its conceptually simple formulation, backpropagating the diffusion loss into the VAE encoder causes severe degradation of the latent space, consistent with observations in prior work [ 33 ] . In our experiments, the vanilla end-to-end setup attains an FID of 33.95 on ImageNet 256 × \times 256 after 80 epochs, which is considerably worse than standard two-stage LDM baselines. We refer this setting as Vanilla E2E .

sections.heading: Why does Vanilla E2E training fail?
sections.text: We observe that vanilla end-to-end training drives the latent space into a highly degenerate representation. To diagnose this phenomenon, we compute the Tweedie estimate of the clean latent 𝐳 ^ 0 = 𝐳 t − t ​ V 𝜽 ​ ( 𝐳 t , t ) \hat{\mathbf{z}}_{0}={\mathbf{z}}_{t}-tV_{\bm{\theta}}({\mathbf{z}}_{t},t) and compare the latent reconstruction error ‖ 𝐳 ^ 0 − 𝐳 0 ‖ 2 \|\hat{\mathbf{z}}_{0}-{\mathbf{z}}_{0}\|^{2} with the corresponding pixel reconstruction error ‖ 𝒟 𝝍 ​ ( 𝐳 ^ 0 ) − 𝐱 0 ‖ 2 \|\mathcal{D}_{{\bm{\psi}}}(\hat{\mathbf{z}}_{0})-{\mathbf{x}}_{0}\|^{2} . As shown in Fig. 3 a, the latent error is nearly zero, whereas the pixel error remains substantial. This indicates that the diffusion model fits its latent-space objective very well, yet the resulting latent code no longer preserves the information required for accurate pixel reconstruction. To further scrutinize this failure mode, we visualize the latent distribution and find that it deviates significantly from a standard Gaussian prior, forming multiple sharp peaks in latent space (see Fig. 3 b). A closer inspection reveals strong per-channel biases and heavily suppressed per-channel variances (see Fig. 3 c). In such a collapsed regime, most latent codes concentrate in a few narrow regions, and the conditional distribution of clean latent 𝐳 0 {\mathbf{z}}_{0} given noisy state 𝐳 t {\mathbf{z}}_{t} becomes extremely concentrated. The diffusion model can then minimize its loss by predicting nearly constant mean values across inputs, because small perturbations around these peaks incur very little error under the diffusion objective. Taken together, these observations suggest that the primary cause of failure is an exploitable latent space: without any pixel-space feedback or explicit regularization, the diffusion model can converge to trivial solutions that achieve low diffusion loss in latent space while discarding the semantic content needed for faithful image reconstruction.

sections.heading: 3.2 Tweedie Pixel Reconstruction Loss
sections.text: The latent collapse observed in vanilla end-to-end training suggests that the diffusion model can exploit the latent space for trivial solution when no pixel-level constraints are provided. To counter this, we strengthen the connection between diffusion predictions and the underlying image content so that the VAE is compelled to maintain a semantically meaningful latent representation. This motivates the Tweedie Pixel Reconstruction (TPR) loss, which decodes the Tweedie-estimated latent back into pixel space and directly enforces consistency with the clean image. Given the stochastic interpolant 𝐳 t = ( 1 − t ) ​ 𝐳 0 + t ​ ϵ {\mathbf{z}}_{t}=(1-t){\mathbf{z}}_{0}+t{\bm{\epsilon}} , the diffusion model estimates the clean latent via Tweedie’s formula 𝐳 ^ 0 = 𝐳 t − t ​ V 𝜽 ​ ( 𝐳 t , t ) \hat{\mathbf{z}}_{0}={\mathbf{z}}_{t}-tV_{\bm{\theta}}({\mathbf{z}}_{t},t) . We decode this estimate using D 𝝍 D_{\bm{\psi}} and penalize discrepancies with the ground-truth image: ℒ TPR ​ ( ϕ , 𝝍 , 𝜽 ) = 𝔼 𝐱 0 , 𝐳 0 , ϵ , t ​ [ ‖ 𝒟 𝝍 ​ ( 𝐳 ^ 0 ) − 𝐱 0 ‖ 2 ] . \mathcal{L}_{\text{TPR}}({\bm{\phi}},{\bm{\psi}},{\bm{\theta}})=\mathbb{E}_{{\mathbf{x}}_{0},{\mathbf{z}}_{0},{\bm{\epsilon}},t}\left[\left\|\mathcal{D}_{{\bm{\psi}}}(\hat{\mathbf{z}}_{0})-{\mathbf{x}}_{0}\right\|^{2}\right]. (2) This objective amounts to a pixel-space MSE and can be further enhanced with perceptual losses such as LPIPS [ 62 ] . We augment the vanilla end-to-end objective in Eq. 1 with the TPR loss. This addition effectively prevents latent collapse (see Fig. 3 ) and substantially improves generation quality, reducing the FID on ImageNet 256 × \times 256 generation from 33.95 to 5.79 after 80 epochs. We refer this setting as E2E w/ TPR Loss .

sections.heading: 3.3 Scaling with Refined Architecture
sections.text: Building on our end-to-end framework, we adopt a vision-transformer-based VAE (ViT-VAE) in place of the conventional convolutional design (CNN-VAE). The encoder employs a patch-embedding layer followed by transformer blocks, and the decoder mirrors this structure. For the diffusion backbone, we refine DiT [ 41 ] with several modern architectural components. Following LighteningDiT [ 58 ] , we integrate RMSNorm, SwiGLU activations, and 2D RoPE, and we replace block-specific modulation layers with a shared global modulation mechanism supplemented by per-block learnable biases, similar to PixArt- α \alpha [ 6 ] . Unless otherwise specified, the patch size is fixed to 1 in all experiments. We refer this as Refined-DiT. Additional architectural details are provided in Sec. A.1 . Employing ViT-VAE and Refined-DiT and training them end-to-end with the TPR loss, this variant reduces computation while improving performance, enabling improved scaling behavior. Model configurations are summarized in Tab. 7 in Appendix. Each training step consists of two decoder passes (for the VAE and the TPR objective) and one encoder and diffusion pass. With these architectural refinements, the total training cost decreases from 436.29 to 334.98 GFLOPs, and the model achieves an improved FID of 3.66 on ImageNet 256 × \times 256 after 80 epochs. We refer to this setting as SpeeDiff (w/o REPA++) to emphasize that it does not require alignment from pretrained VFMs.

sections.text: We first outline the experimental setup in Sec. 4.1 , followed by a controlled component-wise comparison in Sec. 4.2 . sections.heading: Training.
sections.text: We follow the training setup of SiT [ 37 ] and REPA [ 60 ] for ImageNet [ 7 ] 256 × \times 256 generation. The dataset is preprocessed with center cropping [ 17 ] and random horizontal flipping [ 30 ] . All models are trained for 200 epochs (1M iterations) with a batch size of 256, which we find sufficient for SpeeDiff to converge. We use the Adam optimizer [ 27 ] with a constant learning rate of 1e-4 across all components. Exponential moving averages (EMA) [ 44 ] are maintained for ViT-VAE and Refined-DiT with decay rates of 0.999 and 0.9999, respectively. We consider three model scales (B, L, XL) for both ViT-VAE and Refined-DiT, with parameters, FLOPs, and memory consumption summarized in Tab. 7 in Appendix. All ViT-VAE models adopt a 16 × \times spatial compression and a 32 latent channels (f16d32). For 512 × \times 512 generation, we modify only the first patch embedding layer to use 32 × \times spatial compression (f32d32), keeping all other configurations unchanged. We use DINOv3-ViT-L/16 (0.3B) as the default VFM for representation alignment. To ensure reproducibility, we include the training pseudocode in Algorithm 1 in Appendix, and list detailed model configurations and hyperparameters in Tab. 14 in Appendix. Implementation details of all loss objectives are provided in Appendix A .

sections.heading: Sampling.
sections.text: For class-conditioned generation, we adopt the standard Euler–Maruyama SDE solver [ 52 ] with 250 NFEs by default. Guidance sampling uses AutoGuidance (AG) [ 25 ] instead of Classifier-Free Guidance (CFG) [ 21 ] , as we observe that the benefit of CFG diminishes when the diffusion model attains strong unconditional performance with the null-class embedding. AG addresses this issue by leveraging a weaker auxiliary model that does not rely on null-class conditioning. Further implementation details and rationale are discussed in Sec. A.3.1 .

sections.heading: Evaluation.
sections.text: For image generation, following common practice, we report generation Frechet Inception Distance (gFID) [ 20 ] ), spatial FID (sFID) [ 39 ] , Inception Score (IS) [ 47 ] ), precision (Pre.) and recall (Rec.) [ 31 ] , all computed with 50,000 generated samples. Unless specified, all images are generated without guidance. We perform evaluation using the official OpenAI diffusion model evaluation suite [ 8 ] . To assess the reconstruction capability of the VAE, we additionally report the reconstruction FID (rFID) and Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio (PSNR) [ 56 ] . For evaluating semantics of the learned latent space and its alignment to pretrained VFM representations, we further follow REPA [ 60 ] and report linear probing accuracy and the CKNNA score [ 23 ] . sections.heading: 4.2 Component-wise Comparison
sections.text: We begin by examining the contribution of each component and, in particular, the effect of allowing diffusion loss gradients to update the VAE encoder. Beyond the configurations described in Sec. 3 , we introduce more baselines to provide clearer reference points. The first is Two-stage Baseline of LDM, where a convolutional VAE (CNN-VAE) is trained to convergence before training a DiT-XL/1 diffusion model on its latent space. To isolate the effect of end-to-end gradient feedback, we also include a One-stage Baseline in which the VAE and diffusion model are trained jointly from scratch, but a stop-gradient operation prevents diffusion loss from propagating into the VAE encoder. In summary, as shown in Tab. 1 , once TPR loss is applied to prevent latent collapse, end-to-end optimization consistently outperforms both detached variants.

sections.heading: Accelerated convergence.
sections.text: A primary advantage of SpeeDiff lies in its ability to substantially accelerate diffusion model convergence. On ImageNet 256 × \times 256, SpeeDiff-XL (w/ REPA++) reaches a gFID of 7.36 without guidance within 10 epochs, already surpassing the vanilla SiT baseline trained for 1400 epochs. As shown in Tab. 2 , SpeeDiff-XL (w/o REPA++) attains a gFID of 3.66 without guidance after 80 epochs, indicating that allowing diffusion loss gradients to directly shape the latent space significantly improves convergence speed. The incorporation of REPA++ further strengthens this effect, enabling SpeeDiff-XL to reach a gFID of 1.69 without guidance after 80 epochs. SpeeDiff could produce high visual fidelity without guidance, with representative samples presented in Fig. 4 .

sections.heading: Improved scaling behavior.
sections.text: SpeeDiff also induces improved scaling behavior in diffusion models. As shown in Fig. 1 and Tabs. 2 and 3 , SpeeDiff exhibits a clearer and more monotonic scaling trend compared to prior state of the art approaches such as EDM2 [ 26 ] . SpeeDiff adopts a fully transformer based pipeline, which benefits from the strong scaling properties and avoids the capacity limitations of convolution. In addition, SpeeDiff scales the VAE and diffusion model jointly rather than enlarging only the diffusion while keeping the VAE fixed. This joint scaling leads to improved scaling behavior. Further analysis in Sec. B.1 examines parameter allocation across the VAE encoder, VAE decoder, and diffusion model, and shows that appreciate allocation yields consistently stronger performance.

sections.heading: Automatic semantic gain.
sections.text: Analysis of the latent spaces of SpeeDiff (w/o REPA++) and SpeeDiff (w/ REPA++) shows that end-to-end training with diffusion loss gradients naturally smooths the latent and strengthens its semantic organization, as illustrated in Fig. 5 a, where independently trained VAEs tend to overfit low level image statistics and exhibit weak semantic separation. This phenomenon is further supported by the quantitative results in Fig. 5 b, where latent linear probing accuracy on ImageNet improves by 9.45%, indicating that the diffusion objective induces a more semantically aligned latent space.

sections.heading: Generation-friendly latent space.
sections.text: We further examine whether the trained VAE in SpeeDiff remains effective when used separately from the diffusion model it was trained with. We freeze the converged VAE from SpeeDiff-XL (w/ REPA++) and train a new diffusion model from scratch, which converges at a similar speed to SpeeDiff ( Tab. 4 ). This suggests that SpeeDiff learns a generation-friendly latent space. From this perspective, SpeeDiff can be interpreted as performing latent pretraining, producing representations inherently better suited for downstream generative modeling. Model Metrics 4.5 Ablations Components of REPA++. To understand the roles of the two components within REPA++, we evaluate Latent-REPA and Diff-REPA using the CKNNA metric computed with DINOv3-L. Latent-REPA notably improves the semantic alignment of the VAE latent space, although this benefit transfers weakly to the diffusion model. Diff-REPA, on the other hand, substantially improves the alignment of intermediate diffusion features, but the effect diminishes in deeper layers. REPA++ integrates these two components through a simple additive formulation, allowing their strengths to complement each other. As shown in Fig. 5 c, the latent space inherits strong alignment from Latent-REPA, while the diffusion model maintains consistently high alignment across layers due to Diff-REPA. Quantitative results are provided in Tab. 5 . Latent channels. The number of latent channels serves as a key hyperparameter governing the trade-off between reconstruction and generation. Increasing the latent channels generally alleviates the information bottleneck and improves reconstruction. However, excessively large latent channels often lead to a less compact and less semantically structured latent space, making the diffusion model more difficult to train. Across a range of model sizes and settings, we observe that 32 channels consistently yield the best overall performance, shown in Sec. 4.4 . 5 Conclusion In this work, we conduct a detailed analysis of why vanilla end-to-end training of the VAE and diffusion model fails, and identify latent space collapse as the primary cause. By introducing the Tweedie Pixel Reconstruction loss, we establish a stable and effective optimization pathway that enables the VAE to benefit directly from diffusion loss gradient supervision. Building on this foundation, architectural refinements together with the proposed REPA++ further improve convergence speed and generative quality. A.1 Model Details A.1.1 ViT-VAE We adopt a vision-transformer–based VAE (ViT-VAE) in place of the conventional convolutional VAE, as transformer architectures have better scalibility and offer improved compute efficiency (see Tab. 7 for comparison). Encoder. The encoder begins with a patch-embedding layer that tokenizes each p × p p\times p patch into a hidden vector. We use p = 16 p{=}16 for ImageNet 256 × \times 256 and p = 32 p{=}32 for 512 × \times 512 generation. The embedded tokens are processed by a stack of standard transformer blocks equipped with 2D RoPE [ 19 ] positional encoding and SwiGLU [ 48 ] feedforward layers. A final linear projection maps the output tokens into a compact latent representation of dimension d = 32 d{=}32 . Decoder. The decoder mirrors the encoder. It first maps the latent tokens back to the hidden dimension through a linear layer, followed by transformer blocks, and finally an unpatch-embedding layer that reconstructs pixel-space outputs. To further refine visual details, we append a single convolutional layer initialized as an identity mapping. This lightweight refinement consistently improves visual quality. A.1.2 Refined-DiT Our diffusion model, Refined-DiT, is based on recent architectural advances from Lightening DiT [ 58 ] and incorporates a more parameter-efficient modulation mechanism. Due to spatial downsampling introduced by the VAE, we fix the diffusion model’s patch size to 1 1 , implemented as a simple linear projection into the transformer hidden dimension. The model then applies a sequence of diffusion transformer blocks. Instead of per-block modulation, we adopt a global modulation layer combined with learnable per-block biases, following the design strategy of PixArt- α \alpha [ 6 ] . A.3 Sampling Details In this section, we describe our guidance sampling strategy based on AutoGuidance [ 25 ] and discuss how representation alignment affects Classifier-Free Guidance (CFG) [ 21 ] in SpeeDiff. In particular, we analyze why the gains from CFG tend to saturate when REPA++ is enabled. A.3.1 AutoGuidance For all SpeeDiff variants, we train an additional bad version of the diffusion model required by AutoGuidance. Concretely, this bad model is architecturally smaller: it uses half the number of transformer blocks and half the number of attention heads compared to the main model. To decouple it from end-to-end training, we pair this bad diffusion model with the frozen VAE obtained from the 200-epoch checkpoint and train the bad diffusion model from scratch for only 20 epochs. At sampling time, we apply AutoGuidance using this bad model in conjunction with the main model. The guidance scale and guidance intervals are tuned per model size to achieve the best gFID score. A.3.2 Analysis of Unconditional Generation and CFG We compare three settings for guidance: (1) without guidance, (2) CFG, and (3) AutoGuidance (AG). For SpeeDiff (w/ REPA++), we observe that the improvement from CFG over the unguided model is noticeably saturated, whereas AG continues to provide a substantial gain. After careful analysis, we identify a key contributing factor: the unconditional generation of SpeeDiff (with REPA++) is already surprisingly strong. In other words, the null-class (unconditional) predictions of the main model produce high-quality samples. We illustrate unconditional samples in Fig. 6 and report their FID scores in Tab. 9 . Due to the strong unconditional sampling quality, the negative direction in CFG provides only limited additional guidance. AutoGuidance avoids this issue by constructing the negative direction using the prediction of a deliberately degraded bad model under the conditional class. This alternative direction is substantially more informative, and as a result, AutoGuidance delivers a much larger improvement in FID compared to CFG. Unlike prior latent-diffusion pipelines that pair a fixed-size VAE with diffusion models of various capacities, SpeeDiff benefits substantially from joint scaling both components. A larger VAE not only produces a more expressive latent space but also provides stronger feedback to the diffusion model during end-to-end training. To understand how model capacity should be allocated, we systematically vary the number of transformer layers assigned to the encoder, decoder, and diffusion model. As shown in Fig. 7 , several trends emerge. First, the encoder and decoder perform best when their depths are approximately balanced (around a 1:1 ratio). Second, dedicating roughly 40% of total layers to the VAE yields a strong trade-off between reconstruction quality and downstream generative performance. Finally, we observe a consistent and stable scaling trend across model sizes, both with and without REPA++, when following a 1:1:3 allocation rule for encoder, decoder, and diffusion layers. sections.heading: Components of REPA++.
sections.text: To understand the roles of the two components within REPA++, we evaluate Latent-REPA and Diff-REPA using the CKNNA metric computed with DINOv3-L. Latent-REPA notably improves the semantic alignment of the VAE latent space, although this benefit transfers weakly to the diffusion model. Diff-REPA, on the other hand, substantially improves the alignment of intermediate diffusion features, but the effect diminishes in deeper layers. REPA++ integrates these two components through a simple additive formulation, allowing their strengths to complement each other. As shown in Fig. 5 c, the latent space inherits strong alignment from Latent-REPA, while the diffusion model maintains consistently high alignment across layers due to Diff-REPA. Quantitative results are provided in Tab. 5 .

sections.heading: Latent channels.
sections.text: The number of latent channels serves as a key hyperparameter governing the trade-off between reconstruction and generation. Increasing the latent channels generally alleviates the information bottleneck and improves reconstruction. However, excessively large latent channels often lead to a less compact and less semantically structured latent space, making the diffusion model more difficult to train. Across a range of model sizes and settings, we observe that 32 channels consistently yield the best overall performance, shown in Sec. 4.4 .

sections.heading: 5 Conclusion
sections.text: In this work, we conduct a detailed analysis of why vanilla end-to-end training of the VAE and diffusion model fails, and identify latent space collapse as the primary cause. By introducing the Tweedie Pixel Reconstruction loss, we establish a stable and effective optimization pathway that enables the VAE to benefit directly from diffusion loss gradient supervision. Building on this foundation, architectural refinements together with the proposed REPA++ further improve convergence speed and generative quality. Overall, SpeeDiff sets new state-of-the-art results for both non-alignment and VFM-aligned latent diffusion models. Supplementary Material

sections.heading: Appendix A Detailed Implementation of SpeeDiff
sections.text: This section provides comprehensive implementation details of SpeeDiff to ensure full reproducibility. We describe our model architectures in Sec. A.1 , training configurations in Sec. A.2 , and sampling setup in Sec. A.3 . A complete summary of hyperparameters and model configurations is included in Tab. 14 .

sections.heading: A.1.1 ViT-VAE
sections.text: We adopt a vision-transformer–based VAE (ViT-VAE) in place of the conventional convolutional VAE, as transformer architectures have better scalibility and offer improved compute efficiency (see Tab. 7 for comparison).

sections.heading: Encoder.
sections.text: The encoder begins with a patch-embedding layer that tokenizes each p × p p\times p patch into a hidden vector. We use p = 16 p{=}16 for ImageNet 256 × \times 256 and p = 32 p{=}32 for 512 × \times 512 generation. The embedded tokens are processed by a stack of standard transformer blocks equipped with 2D RoPE [ 19 ] positional encoding and SwiGLU [ 48 ] feedforward layers. A final linear projection maps the output tokens into a compact latent representation of dimension d = 32 d{=}32 .

sections.heading: Decoder.
sections.text: The decoder mirrors the encoder. It first maps the latent tokens back to the hidden dimension through a linear layer, followed by transformer blocks, and finally an unpatch-embedding layer that reconstructs pixel-space outputs. To further refine visual details, we append a single convolutional layer initialized as an identity mapping. This lightweight refinement consistently improves visual quality.

sections.heading: A.1.2 Refined-DiT
sections.text: Our diffusion model, Refined-DiT, is based on recent architectural advances from Lightening DiT [ 58 ] and incorporates a more parameter-efficient modulation mechanism. Due to spatial downsampling introduced by the VAE, we fix the diffusion model’s patch size to 1 1 , implemented as a simple linear projection into the transformer hidden dimension. The model then applies a sequence of diffusion transformer blocks. Instead of per-block modulation, we adopt a global modulation layer combined with learnable per-block biases, following the design strategy of PixArt- α \alpha [ 6 ] . The reconstruction 𝐱 ^ vae = D 𝝍 ​ ( 𝐳 0 ) \hat{{\mathbf{x}}}_{\text{vae}}=D_{{\bm{\psi}}}({\mathbf{z}}_{0}) is supervised by a combination of four losses: MSE, LPIPS, discriminator loss, and KL divergence.

sections.heading: MSE Loss.
sections.text: We compute the pixel-wise mean squared error between the clean and reconstructed images. Empirically, MSE and MAE yield similar visual quality, and we adopt MSE by default.

sections.heading: LPIPS Loss.
sections.text: We use the official LPIPS implementation [ 62 ] with a VGG backbone [ 51 ] . LPIPS is computed at the original image resolution without downsampling.

sections.heading: Discriminator Loss.
sections.text: We incorporate a PatchGAN-style discriminator to enhance perceptual fidelity. To ensure stable adversarial training without relying on warm-up schedules or dynamically adjusted weights, we introduce two modifications: • Replace BatchNorm with SpectralNorm [ 38 ] to improve Lipschitz continuity and reduce training instability. • Apply LeCam regularization [ 53 ] , which tracks an exponential moving average of real and fake logits and penalizes large deviations, effectively smoothing discriminator updates. These stabilizations allow us to adopt a fixed discriminator loss weight and enable adversarial supervision from the beginning of training without the need for special scheduling.

sections.heading: Variational Objective (KL Loss).
sections.text: The evidence lower bound (ELBO) [ 28 ] has an additional KL divergence loss between the posterior p ϕ ​ ( 𝐳 0 | 𝐱 0 ) p_{{\bm{\phi}}}({\mathbf{z}}_{0}|{\mathbf{x}}_{0}) and the standard Gaussian prior 𝒩 ⁡ ( 𝟎 , 𝑰 ) \mathcal{N}({\bm{0}},{\bm{I}}) . Interestingly, the KL weight strongly affects the trade-off between reconstruction of VAE and generative of diffusion. As the KL weight increases, reconstruction performance decreases while generative quality initially improves and then degrades. We select the turning point that yields the best generation performance; details are provided in Sec. B.3 .

sections.heading: A.2.5 REPA++
sections.text: We adopt the REPA++ to align both the latent 𝐳 0 {\mathbf{z}}_{0} and intermediate diffusion features 𝐟 t {\mathbf{f}}_{t} extracted from 𝐳 t {\mathbf{z}}_{t} . The adapter is implemented as a two-layer MLP with SiLU activation.

sections.heading: A.2.6 Loss Coefficients
sections.text: SpeeDiff consists of multiple loss components, yet we observe that the model is robust to a wide range of loss weights. Therefore, we adopt simple defaults: all losses use a weight of 1.0 1.0 except the discriminator loss and KL loss, which are set to 0.1 0.1 and 1 × 10 − 5 1\times 10^{-5} , respectively. The discriminator weight improves training stability, while the KL weight is selected based on the analysis in Sec. B.3 .

sections.heading: A.3 Sampling Details
sections.text: In this section, we describe our guidance sampling strategy based on AutoGuidance [ 25 ] and discuss how representation alignment affects Classifier-Free Guidance (CFG) [ 21 ] in SpeeDiff. In particular, we analyze why the gains from CFG tend to saturate when REPA++ is enabled.

sections.heading: A.3.1 AutoGuidance
sections.text: For all SpeeDiff variants, we train an additional bad version of the diffusion model required by AutoGuidance. Concretely, this bad model is architecturally smaller: it uses half the number of transformer blocks and half the number of attention heads compared to the main model. To decouple it from end-to-end training, we pair this bad diffusion model with the frozen VAE obtained from the 200-epoch checkpoint and train the bad diffusion model from scratch for only 20 epochs. At sampling time, we apply AutoGuidance using this bad model in conjunction with the main model. The guidance scale and guidance intervals are tuned per model size to achieve the best gFID score.

sections.heading: A.3.2 Analysis of Unconditional Generation and CFG
sections.text: We compare three settings for guidance: (1) without guidance, (2) CFG, and (3) AutoGuidance (AG). For SpeeDiff (w/ REPA++), we observe that the improvement from CFG over the unguided model is noticeably saturated, whereas AG continues to provide a substantial gain. After careful analysis, we identify a key contributing factor: the unconditional generation of SpeeDiff (with REPA++) is already surprisingly strong. In other words, the null-class (unconditional) predictions of the main model produce high-quality samples. We illustrate unconditional samples in Fig. 6 and report their FID scores in Tab. 9 . Due to the strong unconditional sampling quality, the negative direction in CFG provides only limited additional guidance. AutoGuidance avoids this issue by constructing the negative direction using the prediction of a deliberately degraded bad model under the conditional class. This alternative direction is substantially more informative, and as a result, AutoGuidance delivers a much larger improvement in FID compared to CFG. sections.heading: B.1 Joint Scaling of VAE and Diffusion
sections.text: In this section, we examine how jointly scaling the VAE and the diffusion model affects performance. Unlike prior latent-diffusion pipelines that pair a fixed-size VAE with diffusion models of various capacities, SpeeDiff benefits substantially from joint scaling both components. A larger VAE not only produces a more expressive latent space but also provides stronger feedback to the diffusion model during end-to-end training. To understand how model capacity should be allocated, we systematically vary the number of transformer layers assigned to the encoder, decoder, and diffusion model. As shown in Fig. 7 , several trends emerge. First, the encoder and decoder perform best when their depths are approximately balanced (around a 1:1 ratio). Second, dedicating roughly 40% of total layers to the VAE yields a strong trade-off between reconstruction quality and downstream generative performance. Finally, we observe a consistent and stable scaling trend across model sizes, both with and without REPA++, when following a 1:1:3 allocation rule for encoder, decoder, and diffusion layers. (a) Encoder and decoder perform best with a balanced 1:1 ratio. (b) Allocating about 40% of total layers to the VAE gives a strong trade-off. (c) A 1:1:3 allocation (encoder:decoder:diffusion) consistently works well with and without REPA++.

sections.heading: B.2 SpeeDiff with Conventional Architecture
sections.text: We further evaluate the impact of our refined architectures by comparing ViT-VAE and Refined-DiT with conventional CNN-VAE and DiT variants. As shown in Tab. 10 , both refinements consistently improve performance across model scales. Across both non-aligned and REPA++ settings, our refined architectures provide consistent improvements over conventional CNN-VAE and DiT designs. Without alignment, replacing DiT with Refined-DiT already yields substantial gains (e.g., gFID improves from 5.89 to 3.71 with CNN-VAE), and replacing CNN-VAE with ViT-VAE further enhances performance, reaching 3.66 at the XL scale on ImageNet 256 × \times 256 generation after 80 epochs. With REPA++, the benefits become even more pronounced: Refined-DiT-XL lowers gFID from 2.83 to 2.15, and jointly scaling the VAE achieves the best overall result of 1.69 on ImageNet 256 × \times 256 generation after 80 epochs. Together, these findings confirm the effectiveness of our refined architectures.

sections.heading: B.3 Analysis the Effect of KL Loss

sections.heading: B.5 Analysis of Practical Cost
sections.text: We analyze the practical cost of SpeeDiff by measuring the time-level speedup attributable to end-to-end training. Specifically, we compare SpeeDiff (w/o REPA++) against the two-stage baseline, which assumes a pretrained VAE with preprocessed latents and thus requires only a single diffusion forward pass per training step . In contrast, our end-to-end approach additionally involves one VAE encoder call and two decoder calls per step , resulting in an approximately 2 × \times slower per-step time (see Tab. 13 for detailed per-step timing and Tab. 7 for model FLOPs). Despite this per-step overhead, SpeeDiff converges dramatically faster in terms of training steps. Taking the baseline’s 7.93 FID without guidance at 4M steps as the reference point, SpeeDiff reaches the same FID in only 0.17M steps. This translates to a 23.52 × \times step-level speedup and, after accounting for the per-step cost difference, a 12.14 × \times time-level speedup. Notably, these numbers are conservative: the two-stage pipeline additionally requires VAE pretraining or finetuning as a prerequisite, whereas SpeeDiff trains the VAE jointly from scratch, further widening the practical efficiency gap. In principle, joint training allows the diffusion loss gradient to directly guide the VAE encoder, encouraging the formation of a generation-friendly latent space and potentially yielding faster convergence than the conventional two-stage approach with a pretrained frozen VAE. However, a naive end-to-end implementation severely degrades performance, as unrestricted backpropagation of the diffusion loss leads to latent space collapse. Our main technical contribution is a simple yet effective Tweedie Pixel Reconstruction (TPR) loss, which provides additional pixel-level feedback by decoding a predicted clean latent from an intermediate noisy state using Tweedie’s formula, thereby alleviating collapse. Furthermore, our method enables jointly scaling a fully transformer-based architecture and enhances representation alignment within the end-to-end framework. Our SpeeDiff-XL model achieves over 140 × \times and 61 × \times faster training compared to Vanilla SiT and REPA, respectively, while attaining an FID of 1.50 without guidance on ImageNet 256 × \times 256 generation. With a more efficient 32 × \times compressed VAE, our model further reaches an FID of 1.53 without guidance on ImageNet 512 × \times 512 generation. (a) Conventional two-stage LDM training: a CNN-based VAE [ 28 ] is first trained and then frozen, after which a diffusion (usually a DiT [ 41 ] ) is trained on its latent space. (b) SpeeDiff: a scalable, pixel-anchored end-to-end paradigm that jointly trains the VAE and diffusion model from scratch, without stop-gradient operation, within a fully transformer-based architecture. (c) Training efficiency: on ImageNet 256 × \times 256 generation, SpeeDiff accelerates convergence by over 140 × \times compared to Vanilla SiT and 61 × \times compared to REPA. (d) Scalability: on ImageNet 512 × \times 512 generation, SpeeDiff demonstrates clear scalability with a more efficient 32 × \times compressed VAE with different model size (B, X, XL). 1 1 footnotetext: Work done during internship at ByteDance Seed. 1 Introduction Latent diffusion models (LDMs) [ 54 , 46 , 41 ] have emerged as a dominant paradigm for visual synthesis. These models perform the diffusion process in a compact latent space produced by a visual tokenizer, typically a variational autoencoder (VAE) [ 28 ] . In the standard two-stage training pipeline, the visual tokenizer is first trained to encode raw visual data into a compressed latent space, after which a diffusion model is learned to operate within that latent domain while keeping the pretrained visual tokenizer frozen. Recent advances in LDMs have largely focused on enhancing the VAEs by leveraging vision foundation models (VFMs) [ 40 , 50 , 45 , 61 , 18 ] . Despite their success, VAEs trained with reconstruction objectives primarily capture low-level pixel statistics, resulting in latent spaces that do not directly associate with sufficient semantic knowledge, posing challenges for the diffusion model to learn efficiently. Motivated by semantically rich representations from self-supervise pretrained VFMs, recent works either incorporate representation alignment to a VFM [ 58 , 33 ] or directly replace the VAE encoder with a VFM [ 63 , 49 , 3 , 5 ] . These approaches have achieved remarkable improvements in training efficiency and generative quality. In contrast to improving the visual tokenizer through VFMs, much less attention has been given to enhancing it via end-to-end optimization with direct feedback from the diffusion model training. This idea can in fact be traced back to LSGM [ 54 ] , where the VAE and diffusion model were jointly trained. However, vanilla end-to-end training was found to degrade overall performance, a phenomenon that has also been revisited in recent studies [ 33 ] . We believe that enabling truly end-to-end optimization holds the potential to further push the performance limits of LDMs, yet existing approaches still lack effective mechanisms to support that. In this paper, we focus on the core idea of enhancing the VAE through end-to-end direct gradient feedback from diffusion training , and show that allowing the latent space to evolve under generative supervision further improves both training efficiency and synthesis quality. After carefully analyzing the vanilla end-to-end training, we find that the diffusion loss tends to collapse the latent space into a degenerate representation. Specifically, we observe that the latent statistics exhibit severely suppressed per-channel variances and large per-channel biass (see Fig. 3 ). We further demonstrate that this latent collapse can be effectively alleviated with a simple Tweedie Pixel Reconstruction (TPR) loss, which computes a pixel-level reconstruction loss by decoding the predicted clean latent from an intermediate noisy state using Tweedie’s formula [ 9 ] . Extensive experiments show that this additional pixel-level feedback anchors the VAE and prevents latent degeneracy, resulting in robust and well-converged end-to-end training. Building upon the end-to-end training framework, we further improve latent diffusion model through two enhancements. We first refine the architecture by replacing the conventional convolutional VAE (CNN-VAE) with a vision-transformer-based variant (ViT-VAE) and modernizing the diffusion backbone (DiT [ 41 , 37 ] ) with recent architectural improvements. In addition, inspired by REPA [ 60 , 33 ] , we introduce REPA++ , a enhanced representation alignment method in our end-to-end training that aligns both the latent and the intermediate diffusion features with VFM representations (e.g., DINOv3 [ 50 ] ) and is optimized end-to-end with both diffusion and VAE. Our final method, SpeeDiff, is a single-stage end-to-end latent diffusion framework that jointly trains the VAE and diffusion model from scratch without stop-gradient operations (see Fig. 1 b), simplifying the conventional two-stage pipeline while substantially accelerating diffusion convergence (see Fig. 1 c) and improving scaling effect (see Fig. 1 d). To assess the contribution of representation alignment, we compare SpeeDiff variants with and without REPA++. The model without alignment achieves an FID of 2.42, setting a new state-of-the-art among methods that do not rely on VFM alignment, whereas incorporating REPA++ further reduces the FID to 1.50. Representation from VFMs. Recent studies show that incorporating semantic representations from self-supervise pretrained vision foundation models (VFMs), such as DINO [ 40 , 50 ] , CLIP [ 45 ] and MAE [ 18 ] , can substantially improve the convergence and generative quality of diffusion models. Depending on how VFMs are utilized, existing approaches fall into two main categories: representation alignment and direct representation utilization. The representation alignment family [ 60 , 33 , 58 ] distills VFM semantics by enforcing consistency between latent (or intermediate diffusion features) and VFM representations. To better integrate VFMs into our end-to-end training paradigm as a flexible plug-and-play module, we adopt the representation alignment strategy and introduce REPA++ , an enhanced alignment mechanism in our end-to-end training framework. We first analyze the vanilla end-to-end training ( Sec. 3.1 ) and identify latent collapse as the primary cause of failure. To address this issue, we introduce a simple yet effective Tweedie Pixel Reconstruction loss that provides additional pixel-level feedback ( Sec. 3.2 ). We then enhance the framework with refined architectures and REPA++ ( Sec. 3.3 , Sec. 3.4 ) to accelerate convergence and improve final performance. 3.1 Vanilla End-to-end Training The vanilla end-to-end setup directly couples the VAE and diffusion model by optimizing both objectives simultaneously from scratch: ℒ Vanilla-E2E ​ ( ϕ , 𝝍 , 𝜽 ) = ℒ VAE ​ ( ϕ , 𝝍 ) + ℒ Diff ​ ( ϕ , 𝜽 ) , \mathcal{L}_{\text{Vanilla-E2E}}({\bm{\phi}},{\bm{\psi}},{\bm{\theta}})=\mathcal{L}_{\text{VAE}}({\bm{\phi}},{\bm{\psi}})+\mathcal{L}_{\text{Diff}}({\bm{\phi}},{\bm{\theta}}), (1) where ϕ {\bm{\phi}} , 𝝍 {\bm{\psi}} and 𝜽 {\bm{\theta}} refers to the parameters of VAE encoder, VAE decoder and diffusion, respectively. Despite its conceptually simple formulation, backpropagating the diffusion loss into the VAE encoder causes severe degradation of the latent space, consistent with observations in prior work [ 33 ] . In our experiments, the vanilla end-to-end setup attains an FID of 33.95 on ImageNet 256 × \times 256 after 80 epochs, which is considerably worse than standard two-stage LDM baselines. We refer this setting as Vanilla E2E . Why does Vanilla E2E training fail? We observe that vanilla end-to-end training drives the latent space into a highly degenerate representation. To diagnose this phenomenon, we compute the Tweedie estimate of the clean latent 𝐳 ^ 0 = 𝐳 t − t ​ V 𝜽 ​ ( 𝐳 t , t ) \hat{\mathbf{z}}_{0}={\mathbf{z}}_{t}-tV_{\bm{\theta}}({\mathbf{z}}_{t},t) and compare the latent reconstruction error ‖ 𝐳 ^ 0 − 𝐳 0 ‖ 2 \|\hat{\mathbf{z}}_{0}-{\mathbf{z}}_{0}\|^{2} with the corresponding pixel reconstruction error ‖ 𝒟 𝝍 ​ ( 𝐳 ^ 0 ) − 𝐱 0 ‖ 2 \|\mathcal{D}_{{\bm{\psi}}}(\hat{\mathbf{z}}_{0})-{\mathbf{x}}_{0}\|^{2} . As shown in Fig. 3 a, the latent error is nearly zero, whereas the pixel error remains substantial. This indicates that the diffusion model fits its latent-space objective very well, yet the resulting latent code no longer preserves the information required for accurate pixel reconstruction. To further scrutinize this failure mode, we visualize the latent distribution and find that it deviates significantly from a standard Gaussian prior, forming multiple sharp peaks in latent space (see Fig. 3 b). A closer inspection reveals strong per-channel biases and heavily suppressed per-channel variances (see Fig. 3 c). In such a collapsed regime, most latent codes concentrate in a few narrow regions, and the conditional distribution of clean latent 𝐳 0 {\mathbf{z}}_{0} given noisy state 𝐳 t {\mathbf{z}}_{t} becomes extremely concentrated. The diffusion model can then minimize its loss by predicting nearly constant mean values across inputs, because small perturbations around these peaks incur very little error under the diffusion objective. Taken together, these observations suggest that the primary cause of failure is an exploitable latent space: without any pixel-space feedback or explicit regularization, the diffusion model can converge to trivial solutions that achieve low diffusion loss in latent space while discarding the semantic content needed for faithful image reconstruction. 3.2 Tweedie Pixel Reconstruction Loss The latent collapse observed in vanilla end-to-end training suggests that the diffusion model can exploit the latent space for trivial solution when no pixel-level constraints are provided. To counter this, we strengthen the connection between diffusion predictions and the underlying image content so that the VAE is compelled to maintain a semantically meaningful latent representation. This motivates the Tweedie Pixel Reconstruction (TPR) loss, which decodes the Tweedie-estimated latent back into pixel space and directly enforces consistency with the clean image. The encoder employs a patch-embedding layer followed by transformer blocks, and the decoder mirrors this structure. For the diffusion backbone, we refine DiT [ 41 ] with several modern architectural components. Following LighteningDiT [ 58 ] , we integrate RMSNorm, SwiGLU activations, and 2D RoPE, and we replace block-specific modulation layers with a shared global modulation mechanism supplemented by per-block learnable biases, similar to PixArt- α \alpha [ 6 ] . Unless otherwise specified, the patch size is fixed to 1 in all experiments. We refer this as Refined-DiT. Additional architectural details are provided in Sec. A.1 . Employing ViT-VAE and Refined-DiT and training them end-to-end with the TPR loss, this variant reduces computation while improving performance, enabling improved scaling behavior. A primary advantage of SpeeDiff lies in its ability to substantially accelerate diffusion model convergence. By introducing the Tweedie Pixel Reconstruction loss, we establish a stable and effective optimization pathway that enables the VAE to benefit directly from diffusion loss gradient supervision. Building on this foundation, architectural refinements together with the proposed REPA++ further improve convergence speed and generative quality.
